newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's LVMH clears DFS takeover hurdle.
newsitem.headline: France's LVMH clears DFS takeover hurdle.

text.p: The stock of luxury goods company LVMH surged more than 8 percent Wednesday after a U.S. arbitrator approved the French company's $2.47 billion contested bid for control of the American duty-free chain DFS.
The arbitrator's decision, announced Tuesday, gave DFS shareholders the green light to sell 58.75 percent of the San Francisco-based chain to LVMH despite the opposition of minority shareholders.
"The world's leading luxury goods group thus acquires the world's leading retailer of luxury goods," LVMH said in a statement.
It said the deal would boost its operating profit by around 30 percent and increase sales, which totalled 29.8 billion francs ($5.7 billion) in 1995, by close to 50 percent.
LVMH stock closed up 104 francs ($20) at 1,347 ($259).
"From a strategic point of view, this is an excellent deal. There had been a lot of speculation recently that it might not go through," said an analyst at brokerage firm Natwest Sellier.

The acquisition of DFS reinforces LVMH's presence around the lucrative Pacific Rim and extends its control over the sale of its luxury products, ranging from Moet & Chandon champagnes to Christian Dior perfumes and Louis Vuitton designer luggage.
Last month it announced it was adding the acclaimed Chateau d'Yquem vineyard near Bordeaux to its glittering portfolio.
A much bigger prize, DFS generates $2.9 billion in sales through 180 stores, most of them in the Asia-Pacific market.
Not only was LVMH's stock the star of the Paris bourse Wednesday, but the huge deal also rippled the currency markets.
Some foreign exchange traders said LVMH's purchase of dollars to pay for the stake contributed to the dollar's rise to as high as 5.26 francs from a low of 5.20 on Tuesday.

LVMH said it had paid the bulk of the purchase price, but completion of the deal still hinges on clearance from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission which is examining the antitrust implications of the deal.
Dissident DFS shareholders also signalled they had no intention of leaving quietly and would ensure that LVMH abided by the terms of the arbitration accord.
The accord, drawn up by arbitrator Ira Millstein, stipulates among other things that LVMH must sign an agreement guaranteeing DFS's long-term autonomy.

One of the dissident shareholders, Robert Miller, said in a statement the agreement "imposed stringent conditions on LVMH's ability to achieve synergies at the expense of DFS and its suppliers who compete directly with LVMH products."

He said he and another dissenting shareholder Tony Pilaro "will closely monitor LVMH's adherence to restrictions on integrating DFS into its operations. There are serious antitrust issues, and DFS suppliers have told us they are cooperating with the FTC as it reviews LVMH's recent Hart-Scott-Rodino filing."
LVMH applied for FTC clearance last week under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust law, beginning a process which normally takes around a month.

LVMH, which has a long tradition of allowing its many brands to retain their identities, said it was committed to preserving the autonomy of DFS and that it had invited DFS Chief Executive Officer Myron Ullman to remain in his job.
